dd-corona-1960.t: A plane caught SPY FILM falling from space (1960) #shorts
dd-corona-1960.d:
CORONA was America's first spy satellite program, run by the CIA and the Air Force. On August 18, 1960 its first fully successful mission launched, and the next day an Air Force C-119 caught the falling film capsule in mid-air over the Pacific. That one mission covered more of the Soviet Union than all earlier U-2 flights combined. On February 22, 1995, President Clinton signed Executive Order 12951, and more than 800,000 CORONA photographs were released to the public.

Sources: CIA, 'CORONA: America's First Satellite Program' (1995); NRO, 'CORONA: America's Eyes in Space'; Executive Order 12951 (1995).
Images: U.S. Air Force photo of a C-119J recovering a CORONA capsule (1960); CORONA KH-4B satellite images of Baikonur and Kennedy Space Center; CIA images of the first CORONA mission (all public domain).

dd-northwoods-1962.t: In 1962 the Joint Chiefs proposed FAKE attacks to start a war #shorts
dd-northwoods-1962.d:
On March 13, 1962, the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff sent Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara a memorandum titled 'Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba', now known as Operation Northwoods. It proposed staged incidents that could be blamed on Cuba to justify an invasion. It was signed by the chairman, General Lyman Lemnitzer. The Kennedy administration rejected it, and none of it was carried out. The document was released in 1997 by the JFK Assassination Records Review Board.

Sources: Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum, 13 March 1962 (JCS 1969/321), released 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board; National Archives.
Images: Operation Northwoods memorandum, 13 March 1962; official portrait of Gen. Lyman L. Lemnitzer, U.S. Army (public domain).

dd-azorian-1974.t: The CIA built a ship to STEAL a Soviet submarine #shorts
dd-azorian-1974.d:
In March 1968 the Soviet submarine K-129 sank in the Pacific with all hands, about 16,500 feet down. The CIA built the Hughes Glomar Explorer, publicly described as a deep-sea mining ship for Howard Hughes, to raise it. In the summer of 1974 the ship lifted part of the submarine; the rest broke away on the way up. The bodies of six Soviet sailors were buried at sea with military honors. When reporters asked, the CIA would 'neither confirm nor deny' the operation, the origin of the 'Glomar response'. The CIA released its own history of Project AZORIAN in 2010.

Sources: CIA, 'Project AZORIAN: The Story of the Hughes Glomar Explorer' (released January 2010); CIA Museum, Project AZORIAN.
Images: CIA Museum images of Project AZORIAN; USNS Glomar Explorer, U.S. Navy photo; Hughes Glomar Explorer crew patch (public domain).

dd-hottel-1950.t: The FBI's most viewed file is about FLYING SAUCERS #shorts
dd-hottel-1950.d:
The most viewed document in the FBI Vault, the Bureau's online reading room, is a one-page memo dated March 22, 1950, from Guy Hottel, head of the Washington field office, to Director J. Edgar Hoover. It passes on a story told by an 'investigator for the Air Forces' about three flying saucers recovered in New Mexico, each with three small bodies inside. The memo itself says no further evaluation was attempted. In 2013 the FBI explained that the memo is not proof of UFOs, but a second- or third-hand claim it never investigated, and that it has no connection to Roswell.

Sources: FBI Records: The Vault, Guy Hottel memo (22 March 1950); FBI statement 'UFOs or No? The Guy Hottel Memo' (March 2013).
Images: Guy Hottel memorandum, 22 March 1950, FBI (public domain).
